about: Nine Tails 새 쇼츠 라인업(2026-10-09 사용자: 한국 설화·조선 금지 · 타깃 해외 영어권 20–39). 2주 시험 10/13–10/26 공개, 10/27 판정. 루틴은 `python gumiho/tales/rules.py next --date <오늘>` 이 준 편을 전부 쓴다(보통 A 1 + B 1). 공개일 = first_publish 부터: survival 매일(offset 0, every 1) · compare 짝수 날(offset 0, every 2) · liminal 홀수 날(offset 1, every 2). 쓰는 날 = 공개 전날(write_ahead_days). facts 는 확인된 수치(fact 마다 src = sources 번호) — 대본의 숫자는 여기서만, 출처 URL 은 여기 것만. careful 은 단정하면 안 되는 것. 판정 뒤 주간 검토가 PR 로 채운다.
slots_note: A 20:00 UTC = 16:00 ET · B 23:30 UTC = 19:30 ET(미국 73% — 하교·퇴근 뒤). 사용자 10/9 결정.

survival.playlist_desc: Dropped into the most extreme places in the universe with a clock running. Real numbers, real sources, one verdict: Gumi's odds. A new part every day.

compare.playlist_desc: Real measurements, drawn to scale and ranked from small to absurd, with a twist at the end. Sources in every description.

liminal.playlist_desc: Original fiction: rules for empty places at 3 A.M. Malls, gas stations, hotel hallways. Follow them in order. Narrated by Gumi.

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on the Floor of the Mariana Trench?

facts.fact: Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench, is approximately 10,935 meters (35,876 feet) deep: nearly 11 kilometers.
Pressure at the bottom of the Mariana Trench is more than 16,000 PSI, against 14.7 PSI at home: about 8 tons on every square inch (derived, US tons).
That is over 1,000 times the standard pressure at sea level.

Pressure rises by 1 atmosphere for every 10.06 meters (33 feet) of depth; by Boyle's law, gas in your lungs shrinks as pressure rises, to roughly 1/1,000 of its size at 1,000 times the pressure (derived).
Below 1,000 meters no sunlight gets through at all (the aphotic zone).
A NOAA instrument measured 2.4 °C water on the floor of Challenger Deep, at 10,646 meters.
A titanium-cased NOAA hydrophone recorded sound on the floor for 23 days: earthquakes, whale moans and a passing typhoon.

beat_ideas.what: you wake up on the floor, 10,935 m down
pitch black: sunlight gave up at 1,000 m; the water is 2.4 °C
more than 16,000 PSI: about 8 tons on every square inch
over 1,000 times surface pressure: the air in your lungs squeezed to a thousandth
comparison for Gumi's line: a titanium NOAA microphone lasted 23 days down here

careful: Death is effectively instant: no source gives seconds-to-death, so don't invent one
'8 tons per square inch' is derived from 16,000 PSI (US tons)
Depth varies by survey (10,935-10,994 m): say 'about'
No gore; don't name people who made dives

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on Mars Without a Spacesuit?

facts.fact: Mars surface pressure averages 6.36 millibars, varying from 4.0 to 8.7 mb with the seasons.
The atmospheric pressure on Mars is around 0.6 percent of Earth's.

Below the Armstrong limit of 47 mmHg (about 6.3 kPa, above 63,000 ft on Earth), body water at 37 °C starts to vaporize; Mars at about 4.8 mmHg is roughly a tenth of that limit (10 times lower, derived).
FAA: above 43,000 ft, useful consciousness lasts only about 9-12 seconds, the time blood takes to travel from lungs to brain.
Mars air is 95.1% carbon dioxide and only 0.16% oxygen.
The average temperature on Mars is about -59 °C (214 K); at the Viking 1 site it swung from -89 °C to -31 °C in a day.
Curiosity measured an average of 0.67 millisieverts of radiation per day on the surface of Mars.

beat_ideas.what: you step out: the air pressure is 0.6% of Earth's
the air is 95.1% CO2 and 0.16% oxygen: nothing to breathe
10 times below the Armstrong limit: the water on your tongue and eyes starts to vaporize
about 9-12 seconds: useful consciousness is gone
for Gumi's line: -59 °C average and 0.67 mSv of radiation a day

careful: Don't say blood boils or bodies explode: tissue water vaporizes
The FAA 9-12 s figure is for altitude above 43,000 ft: say 'like'
Don't mention the 1960s vacuum-chamber accident (a named real person)

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last in the Age of T. Rex?

facts.fact: Tyrannosaurus rex was about 13 meters long, with an estimated bite force of 8,526 to 34,522 newtons: about the weight of 3.5 tonnes (derived).
A 2017 PeerJ simulation found adult T. rex leg bones would have limited it to walking gaits, not running.
Reported top speed from that 2017 study: around 12 miles per hour (about 20 km/h).
70 million years ago a day lasted only 23.5 hours (23 and a half), and a year had 372 days.
The asteroid that ended the age of dinosaurs had a diameter of more than 10 km.
The Chicxulub impact is dated to 66,038,000 years ago, plus or minus 11,000 years.

beat_ideas.what: a year here has 372 days
something 13 meters long is watching you
it can probably only walk, about 12 mph tops: but if it catches you, up to 34,522 newtons of bite
survive the day? a day here is only 23.5 hours

careful: Bite force is a model estimate: give the range or say 'up to'
T. rex speed is debated: say 'probably' and 'about 12 mph'
Day length is measured for 70 million years ago
No gore: imply, don't show
T. rex lived near the very end of the Cretaceous: don't give an exact 'years ago' number

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on Top of Everest Without Oxygen?

facts.fact: Everest's official height is 8,848.86 meters (29,031.69 feet), declared by China and Nepal in December 2020.
At the summit, breathable oxygen is one-third (1/3) of what it is at sea level.
Air pressure at the summit is about 253 mmHg, about 33% of sea level's 760 mmHg (derived).
FAA time of useful consciousness: 2.5-3 minutes at 28,000 ft (1-1.5 minutes after a rapid decompression), and 1-2 minutes at 30,000 ft (30 seconds to 1 minute rapid).
FAA: useful-consciousness time does not mean the onset of unconsciousness; impairment can start at once.
Summit temperatures average -36 °C in January and can drop to -60 °C, with sustained winds of more than 160 km/h (100 mph).
Even climbers acclimatized for weeks had a mean arterial oxygen pressure of only 24.6 mmHg at 8,400 meters.

beat_ideas.what: teleported to 8,848.86 m: each breath holds one-third of the oxygen
-36 °C in January, winds over 160 km/h
sudden exposure this high: useful consciousness can go in 30 seconds (FAA, 30,000 ft)
upper end of the window at 28,000 ft: 1.5 minutes
even with a slow onset, the FAA gives 2.5-3 minutes

careful: FAA times are for a resting, unacclimatized person and mean 'can still act', not death: say so
Real climbers survive because they acclimatize for weeks and usually use bottled oxygen: say so
Don't name climbers or real deaths
'Death zone above 8,000 m' was not verified: don't use the term

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on the Surface of Venus?

facts.fact: Venus' surface pressure is 92 bars, and its average surface temperature is 464 °C (737 K).
The surface pressure is about 93 times Earth's, the same force as being more than 3,000 feet underwater; temperatures are hot enough to melt lead, under dense clouds of sulfuric acid.
Venus' air is 96.5% carbon dioxide and 3.5% nitrogen.
By Boyle's law, air spaces in your body shrink to about 1/92 of their size at 92 bars (derived).
The Soviet Venera 13 lander survived on the surface for 2 hours, 7 minutes (127 minutes).
Sunrise to sunset on Venus would take 117 Earth days.

beat_ideas.what: you land: 92 bars, like being more than 3,000 feet underwater
the air in your lungs squeezed to about 1/92
464 °C: hot enough to melt lead
your gasp is 96.5% carbon dioxide
for Gumi's line: the toughest lander lasted 127 minutes; sunset is 117 days away

careful: Temperatures vary by source (464-467 °C): say 'about'
The acid clouds are high up: don't say acid rain hits you on the ground
Venera 13 is a spacecraft (fine to name)

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last in an Antarctic Winter With No Shelter?

facts.fact: The world's coldest recorded air temperature is -89.2 °C (-128.6 °F), at Vostok station on 21 July 1983.
Satellites show the coldest spots on the East Antarctic Plateau reach -98 °C (-144 °F) at the snow surface.
In the interior the coldest months average -40 to -70 °C; South Pole winter winds average about 17 mph (8 m/s).
National Weather Service: at a -19 °F wind chill exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes; the chart's coldest band is frostbite in 5 minutes, and Antarctic wind chills go beyond the chart.
Hypothermia means a body temperature below 35 °C (95 °F).
Winter at the South Pole brings six months (6) of darkness.

beat_ideas.what: dropped on the plateau: a winter month averages -40 to -70 °C
a 17 mph wind pushes the wind chill off the weather service chart
exposed skin freezes in 5 minutes or less
within hours your core drops below 35 °C: hypothermia
for Gumi's line: Vostok hit -89.2 °C; sunrise is 6 months away

careful: -89.2 °C is the thermometer record; -98 °C is a satellite reading of the snow surface: say 'satellites measured'
Wind chill beyond the chart is an extrapolation: say 'off the chart'
No source for time to hypothermia: say 'within hours', no exact time

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Falling Into a Black Hole?

facts.fact: NASA's 2024 plunge simulation uses a black hole of 4.3 million solar masses, like the one at the Milky Way's center, starting about 640 million km (400 million miles) away.
The fall to the event horizon takes about 3 hours, making nearly two 30-minute orbits on the way.
That event horizon spans about 25 million kilometers (16 million miles); a NASA scientist says that, given the choice, you want to fall into a supermassive black hole.
Once across the horizon, spaghettification destroys the falling camera just 12.8 seconds later, with 128,000 kilometers (79,500 miles) still to go to the singularity.
For a small black hole of 8 solar masses, tides become fatal about 400 km from the center, far outside its 24 km horizon: you are torn apart before you even get in.
For a 30-solar-mass black hole, the trip from horizon to singularity takes 0.000197 seconds of your own time.

beat_ideas.what: 640 million km out from a black hole of 4.3 million suns (in a spacesuit)
one 30-minute orbit as you fall
about 3 hours: you cross the 25-million-km horizon and feel nothing special
12.8 seconds later: spaghettified, 128,000 km short of the center

careful: Assume a spacesuit (vacuum alone kills in about a minute): say 'in a suit'
The 12.8 s is NASA's simulated trajectory: say 'in NASA's simulation'
Don't claim the real Sagittarius A* is survivable (hot gas, radiation are not modeled)
The small-hole contrast (400 km) can be the twist

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last in Death Valley in July Without Water?
survival.situation: DEATH VALLEY IN JULY, NO WATER

facts.fact: July at Furnace Creek averages a high of 116 °F (47 °C); the officially recorded air record is 134 °F (57 °C) on July 10, 1913.
The highest ground temperature recorded at Furnace Creek was 201 °F (about 94 °C), on July 15, 1972.
The park service says to drink at least one gallon of water a day.
Physical work in heat can push sweat loss up to 2 litres per hour.
Past about 5% of body weight lost as fluid come headache and light-headedness; at about 8-10% come weakness, dizziness and faintness.
Heatstroke means a body temperature above 104 °F (40 °C), and at that point sweating may stop.
In heat stroke, body temperature can rise to 106 °F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes.
Summer nights in Death Valley may only cool to 85 °F to 95 °F.

beat_ideas.what: 116 °F on an average July afternoon; the ground can hit 201 °F
the park says drink a gallon a day; you have none
walking for help you sweat up to 2 litres an hour: past 5% fluid loss, headache
8-10% loss: weak, dizzy, fainting
heatstroke: over 104 °F, sweating stops; 106 °F within 10 to 15 minutes

careful: The 134 °F record is official but debated: say 'officially recorded'
Hour beats are estimates for a walking adult: keep words like 'about'
No real Death Valley casualties

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Falling Into Jupiter?

facts.fact: At Jupiter's 1-bar cloud tops it is 165 K (-108 °C) and gravity is 2.36 times Earth's (23.12 m/s²).
Jupiter's air is about 89.8% hydrogen and 10.2% helium, with no breathable oxygen.
Jupiter doesn't have a true surface, and equatorial winds reach up to 335 mph (539 km/h).
Breathing oxygen-free gas can cause unconsciousness after only one or two breaths.
NASA's Galileo probe parachuted into Jupiter in 1995 and returned data for 58 minutes before the pressure (22.7 atmospheres) ended it.
Galileo measured a deep atmosphere of 429 K (about 156 °C) at 22 bars.
Deeper down, Jupiter's pressure and temperature crush, melt and vaporize spacecraft.

beat_ideas.what: dropped at the cloud tops: -108 °C
2.36 times your weight, and nothing solid below
winds of up to 539 km/h
one or two breaths of 89.8% hydrogen and you're out
for Gumi's line: the Galileo probe lasted 58 minutes, down to 22.7 atmospheres and about 156 °C

careful: The 58 minutes is the Galileo probe's parachute descent: say 'the probe lasted 58 minutes', not you
Final pressure varies (22-24 bar): use 22.7 atmospheres
Radiation is an orbit hazard, not part of the drop

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last in the Last Ice Age?

facts.fact: At the Last Glacial Maximum the world was on average 6.1 °C colder than pre-industrial times (95% range 5.7 to 6.5 °C).
Sea level was about 125 meters below today's at the last glacial maximum, about 20,000 years ago.
The Laurentide Ice Sheet over North America reached 2,400 to 3,000 meters (8,000 to 10,000 feet, about 3 km) thick or more, as far south as 37° N.
Woolly mammoths stood about 3 to 3.7 meters tall and weighed 5,500 to 7,300 kg; they became largely extinct about 10,000 years ago.
Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, are dated to about 22,860 and 21,130 years ago, beside tracks of giant ground sloths and dire wolves.
Homo sapiens evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago.

beat_ideas.what: 20,000 years ago: the planet is 6.1 °C colder on average
the beach is 125 m lower: you're standing on future seafloor
up north, ice up to 3 km thick; nearby, a 3.7-meter woolly mammoth
fresh human footprints in the mud: people live here, next to giant sloths and dire wolves

careful: -6.1 °C is a global average: local cooling was bigger
Ice thickness is for the sheet at its largest
White Sands dates were debated: say 'dated to about 21,000-23,000 years ago'
'Humans survived it' is an inference: say 'people lived through it'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last on Titan Without a Spacesuit?

facts.fact: Titan's surface pressure is about 60 percent greater than Earth's, so your blood won't boil, and the temperature is -179 °C (-290 °F).
Titan's air is about 95 percent nitrogen and 5 percent methane.
Oxygen is absent on Titan (it makes up 21% of Earth's air), gravity is 1/7th of Earth's and the air is four times denser.
Breathing oxygen-free gas can cause unconsciousness after only one or two breaths; with 4-6% oxygen a person falls into a coma in less than 40 seconds.
ESA's Huygens probe landed on Titan on 14 January 2005 and kept working on the surface for 1 hour and 10 minutes.
With protective gear and wings on your arms, NASA says you could flap and fly, because the atmosphere is so dense.

beat_ideas.what: no pressure suit needed: 60% more pressure than Earth; -179 °C
1/7th of your weight, in air four times denser
one or two breaths of nitrogen and methane, zero oxygen: you collapse
coma in under 40 seconds (and Titan has 0% oxygen, not 4-6%)
for Gumi's line: Huygens outlasted you, 1 hour 10 minutes on this ground (and with a mask and wings you could fly)

careful: Methane is not the killer, the missing oxygen is
No source for freezing time: don't give one
The wings line is NASA education material: say 'NASA says you could'

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Lost at Sea on a Raft?
survival.situation: ADRIFT ON A RAFT, NO WATER

facts.fact: The ocean surface ranges from about 30°C (86°F) in the tropics to about -2°C (28°F) near the poles.
Unprotected skin can be damaged by the sun's UV rays in as little as 15 minutes, and UV reflects off water.
About 3.5 percent of the weight of seawater is dissolved salt (about 35 parts per thousand).
Kidneys can only make urine less salty than seawater, so to get rid of the salt you drink you have to urinate more water than you drank.
A resting person in a survival situation needs at least about 1 litre of water a day.
Losing more than about 5% of body weight as fluid brings headache and light-headedness; at about 8-10% come weakness, dizziness and fainting.
Death usually comes with acute losses of 15-20% of body water, which can happen in as little as 3 days in hot climates.

beat_ideas.what: tropical sea about 30 °C, no shade, no water
UV is already damaging your skin (15 minutes), and the water reflects it
you need about 1 litre a day; seawater is 3.5% salt: drinking it makes you pee out more than you drank
past 5% fluid loss: headache, light-headed
15-20% loss can kill in as little as 3 days in this heat

careful: Survival time varies with heat: say 'as little as 3 days', not a fixed day
Beat DAY 2 is an estimate: say 'by day two' loosely
No real castaways

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Inside the Sun's Corona?

facts.fact: On Dec. 24, 2024, Parker Solar Probe flew 3.8 million miles (about 6.1 million km) from the Sun's surface, inside the corona.
The corona reaches up to 3.5 million °F (2 million °C).
The corona is about 10 million times less dense than the Sun's surface, so few particles carry that heat to you.
At Parker's closest approach the Sun is about 475 times brighter than at Earth's orbit.
Exposed to space without a suit, you would probably stay conscious for only about the first 9 to 11 seconds; the water on your tongue begins to boil.
Within 1 minute in vacuum, blood would no longer circulate.
Parker's 4.5-inch carbon heat shield withstands nearly 2,500 °F (1,377 °C) while the probe moves at up to 430,000 mph (692,000 km/h).
Parker Solar Probe reaches speeds up to 430,000 mph (692,000 kph).

beat_ideas.what: 6.1 million km from the Sun, in a corona of 2 million °C
but it's 10 million times thinner than the surface: it's the light that gets you
sunlight 475 times stronger than on Earth
about 9 to 11 seconds: you black out; the water on your tongue boils
within 1 minute, your blood stops circulating
for Gumi's line: Parker zips past at 692,000 km/h behind a shield rated to 1,377 °C

careful: Don't say the corona gas burns you: it is too thin; the light and the vacuum get you
No claim about how fast a body vaporizes
Shield temperatures vary across NASA pages: use 1,377 °C rating

survival.title_idea: How Long Would You Last Falling Into Neptune?

facts.fact: At Neptune's 1-bar cloud level it is 72 K (-201 °C), and gravity there is 1.12 times Earth's.
Neptune does not have a solid surface, and its winds whip at more than 1,200 mph (2,000 km/h).
Neptune's air is about 80% hydrogen, 19% helium and 1.5% methane, with no oxygen.
Breathing oxygen-free gas can cause unconsciousness after only one or two breaths.
Neptune's 'surface' pressure is far above 1,000 bars; 80% or more of the planet's mass is a hot, dense fluid of icy materials.
Neptune's Great Dark Spot storm was large enough to contain the entire Earth; Neptune orbits about 4.5 billion km (2.8 billion miles) from the Sun.

beat_ideas.what: dropped at the cloud tops: -201 °C
you weigh about the same as on Earth (1.12 times), but there is nothing to stand on
winds of more than 2,000 km/h grab you
one or two breaths of 80% hydrogen and 19% helium, no oxygen: you're out
for Gumi's line: below you, more than 1,000 bars and a hot, dense fluid of ices

careful: The deep 'ocean' is a model: say 'scientists think'
Wind speeds are at cloud level
Different from Jupiter: focus on the cold (-201 °C), the winds (2,000 km/h) and normal gravity

compare.title_idea: Deep Sea Creatures Ranked by Size Pt.1

facts.fact: The largest known female black seadevil anglerfish is only about 12 centimeters (120 mm standard length); males are under 3 centimeters (28 mm).
The vampire squid grows to about 30 centimeters and lives 600 to 900 meters down.
The deep-sea giant isopod, a relative of the pill bug, grows up to a foot and a half: about 46 centimeters.
The colossal squid at Te Papa measures 4.2 meters but weighs 495 kilograms, the heaviest squid known (shorter, heavier).
The Greenland shark reaches about 6.4 meters (640 cm, 21 feet).
Female giant squid can reach about 13 meters (43 feet) including their two long tentacles.
A giant siphonophore filmed off Western Australia in 2020 was estimated at about 46 meters (150 feet): a colony of tiny linked bodies, not one animal.
The biggest blue whales (Antarctic) reach about 110 feet, or 33.5 meters.

compare.twist_idea: GIANT SIPHONOPHORE about 46 m (estimated): the bar breaks the chart; longer than the biggest blue whale (33.5 m) and it isn't even one animal.
careful: Lengths are measured differently (standard length, tentacles included): say 'about'
Colossal squid is shorter but heavier than the giant squid: say so
Siphonophore length is an estimate

compare.title_idea: Black Holes Ranked by Size Pt.2

facts.fact: Cygnus X-1, the first black hole ever identified, has about 21 times the mass of the Sun (21.2 plus or minus 2.2).
Gaia BH3, about 2,000 light-years away, is the heaviest known stellar black hole in our galaxy: 33 times the Sun's mass.
Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of the Milky Way, has about 4.3 million times the mass of the Sun.
M87*, the first black hole ever photographed (2019), has about 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun.
TON 618, one of the heaviest black holes known, is estimated at more than 60 billion solar masses.
To become a black hole, Earth would have to be crushed to a radius of about 9 millimeters, a ball about 2 centimeters across; the Sun to about 2.95 km.

compare.twist_idea: No value. EARTH AS A BLACK HOLE: crushed to about 2 cm across (9 mm radius).
careful: Mass in suns, not width: say 'by mass'
TON 618 is an estimate: say 'estimated'
M87* also has a 5.4 billion estimate (NASA 2023): say 'about'

compare.title_idea: The Deepest Holes on Earth, Ranked Pt.3

facts.fact: Utah's Bingham Canyon copper pit, the deepest open-pit mine, is more than 1.2 kilometers deep and about 4 kilometers wide.
In 2018 cavers reached 2,212 meters (about 2.2 km) down in Veryovkina Cave in the Caucasus, one of the two deepest known caves.
Mponeng in South Africa, the deepest mine, works gold from 3,160 to 3,740 meters (about 3.7 km) below the surface.
The Challenger Deep, the ocean's deepest point, is about 10,935 meters (about 10.9 km) below the sea surface.
The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 meters (about 12.3 km) straight down, the deepest hole humans have made.
The Kola borehole is only about 23 centimeters (9 inches) wide.

compare.twist_idea: No value. The deepest hole ever dug is only 23 cm wide: you couldn't fit your head in it.
careful: Deepest cave record is contested (Krubera vs Veryovkina): say 'one of the deepest caves'
Kola is the deepest straight down (an oil well is longer in total drilled length)
Challenger Deep is natural and measured from sea level

compare.title_idea: Storms of the Solar System Ranked by Size Pt.4

facts.fact: Typhoon Tip (1979), the largest tropical cyclone on record, had gale-force winds 1,100 km from its center: about 2,200 km across.
Neptune's Great Dark Spot, seen by Voyager 2 in 1989, was about 13,000 km by 6,600 km.
In April 2017 Jupiter's Great Red Spot measured 16,350 kilometers wide (10,159 miles), 1.3 times the width of Earth.
The six-sided jet stream at Saturn's north pole is about 30,000 kilometers (20,000 miles) across.
In the late 1800s the Great Red Spot was up to 25,500 miles (about 41,000 km) long; it has been shrinking ever since.
Earth's mean radius is 6,371 km, so Earth is about 12,742 km wide.

compare.twist_idea: RED SPOT IN THE 1800S, about 41,000 km long: the bar breaks the chart. It is shrinking, yet Earth (12,742 km) still fits inside today.
careful: Typhoon size is the gale-wind field; planet storms are the visible cloud: say 'about'
Neptune's spot has since disappeared
The 1800s figure is the long axis: say 'long', not 'wide'

compare.title_idea: The Biggest Living Things on Earth, Ranked Pt.5

facts.fact: The biggest elephant on record, an African savanna bull, weighed about 24,000 pounds (10,886 kg, about 10.9 tonnes).
Antarctic blue whales can weigh up to 330,000 pounds, about 150 tonnes.
The trunk alone of General Sherman, the largest tree by volume, weighs nearly 1,400 tons (about 1,270 tonnes).
Pando, one aspen in Utah that looks like a forest of more than 47,000 trunks, weighs an estimated 13 million lbs (5.9 million kg, about 5,900 tonnes) and covers some 106 acres (43 ha).
One honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Blue Mountains spreads underground across about 965 hectares, more than 20 times Pando's area, and nobody can weigh it.

compare.twist_idea: No value. HONEY FUNGUS: 965 hectares underground, too big to weigh.
careful: Ranked by weight: say 'by weight'
Pando's weight is an estimate
Sherman is the trunk only

compare.title_idea: The Tallest Mountains in the Solar System, Ranked Pt.6

facts.fact: Mount Everest's summit is 8,848 meters (about 8.8 km) above sea level.
Measured from its base on the seafloor, Mauna Kea rises more than 10,210 meters (about 10.2 km), taller than Everest.
Maxwell Montes, the highest mountain on Venus, rises to an elevation of 11.5 km.
On the asteroid Vesta, a mountain rises about 15 kilometers (9 miles) above the floor of a giant crater.
Olympus Mons on Mars, the largest volcano in the solar system, has an average elevation of 22 km.
The base of Olympus Mons covers an area as large as the US state of Arizona.

compare.twist_idea: No value. OLYMPUS MONS' BASE IS THE SIZE OF ARIZONA.
careful: Heights are measured from different baselines: say 'measured different ways'
Olympus Mons varies by source (22 km per ESA): say 'about'

compare.title_idea: The Fastest Things in the Universe, Ranked Pt.7

facts.fact: Voyager 1 is leaving the solar system at about 17.0 kilometers per second (38,026 mph), about 61,000 km/h.
Earth circles the Sun at an average 29.78 km per second, about 107,000 km/h.
At its closest pass, the Parker Solar Probe moves at approximately 430,000 mph (700,000 km/h), the fastest human-made object.
The solar system circles the Milky Way at about 450,000 mph (720,000 km/h); one lap takes about 230 million years.
Light travels at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, about 1.08 billion km/h.
Sunlight takes about 499 seconds (about 8 minutes 19 seconds) to reach Earth.

compare.twist_idea: No value. The sunlight you see is about 8 minutes old.
careful: km/h values are conversions: say 'about'
Sunlight travel time varies over the year: say 'about 8 minutes'

liminal.title_idea: RULES to Follow if You Wake Up in an Empty Mall at 3 A.M.
liminal.premise: You fell asleep on a bench in a shopping mall. You wake at 3 A.M. The music is still playing. Every store is lit and empty.
liminal.setting: a huge two-floor shopping mall at night: lit storefronts with no people, a dry fountain, escalators running, soft music from ceiling speakers
seeds: the escalators keep running — only ride the one going down
if the music stops, stand still until it starts again
don't look at the mannequins in the store windows twice
